chapter: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
title: Bob-Lo boats and the band that became Casa Loma
summary: While Goldkette was away, Challis wrote for a Detroit band playing the Bob-Lo boats that later became the Casa Loma orchestra.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional

blocks.x: But in those days, some of those tunes could go for a year, year and a half, two years without -- no problem whatever. Well, anyway, I didn't get out on the road at all with them and it seemed like there were no tunes required for the trip and I was asked to, by a guy in the office there if I wouldn't go down -- well, he went to Jean -- if I wouldn't go down on these boats, they had boats running down to a place called [Bob Lo] which is a little below Detroit. There was sort of a picnic ground down there and you go down the Detroit River to this thing. It's about an hour or so trip and they had a band there, and they'd play on the way down, and on the way back we'd rehearse.
So, okay, I went there and made a few trips down and made a few arrangements, made a few trips down and it happened to be the Casa Loma, which was not then the Casa Loma.
They came out of Canada. Originally.
Well, they were Detroit, all Detroit.
Well, they became the Casa Loma when they played at the Casa Loma, in Toronto.

At the Casa Loma outside of Toronto, right, so what the guy's name now, the head of it, the trumpet player. He had a desk in Goldkette's office and used to book these jobs and he'd keep these guys for as much as he could on the same job. So they got this job for the summer there, going down to [Bob Lo] and then in August, of course, the band went to Atlantic City where I was supposed to go.

I am trying to think of the guy's name, but I can't now, but he had the band. He was the trumpet player who had running this thing up in the band and he got the job as I understand it, at Toronto for this Casa Loma, later on, and he went up there and I guess his band was successful and they stayed up there and they took the name of the place, which was Casa Loma, and became the Casa Loma band about a year or so later.
Where did Glen Gray come in?
Well, he was the saxophone player, but he was --
He wasn't the leader then.

That was much later on. It became a cooperative band. The name is on the tip of my tongue, but they got him out and he had the band and they had all -- they had Tony Brilia (brass) they had a lot of guys that didn't stay after it became cooperative, the bass player, the piano player --
Kenny Sargent.
No.
He hadn't come yet.
He didn't come till later. He's very good. These were guys that were playing jobs around Detroit. There was another guy that played there, he wasn't in that band, but I wouldn't be at all surprised.

Also, I think they called them the Orange Blossoms at that time and they played also, opposite the band, the relief band in the Grays tone. That was one of their jobs and Bob Chester was also -- he's from Detroit, he had a band later on.
I remember.

Well, he was a tenor saxophone player out of Detroit. He played around -- Jean had quite a business working up there. And it was evidently failing, that is, not only from Jean, all of them. It was undergoing a change.
Then when radio got big, radio was a boost to the bands, because you would hear them all over the country.
Right, when they began to use it that way. But at the beginning people wanted to buy radios, I guess, to be entertained.
Stay home.
Right.
